title: Despite their differences the Reformed accept Bellarmine's definition of free choice, as Baron, Pareus and Ames show
source_text: XLVIII. Caeterum utcunque inter se varient Scholae Reformatae Doctores, in explicando quae sit natura libertatis, & quibus facultatibus conveniat, aut non conveniat; nihilominus facile admittunt definitionem liberi Arbitrii quae traditur a Bellarmino, De Gratia & libero Arbitrio lib. 3. cap. 3. Nempe quod Liberum Arbitrium est libera potestas ex his quae ad finem aliquem conducunt unum prae alio eligendi, aut unum & idem respuendi, vel acceptandi, pro arbitrio nostro, intelligenti naturae, ad magnam Dei gloriam attributa, vel concessa. Id videre est apud Rob. Baronium in Metaphysica sua generali, sect. 12. Disp. de Libertate Arbitrii, ubi hanc definitionem non solum probat, sed etiam per partes accurate explicat. Eandem quoque definitionem non improbat Paraeus, quandoquidem quibusdam in eam animadversis, fatetur de libero Arbitrio absolute considerato, inter nos & Bellarminum nullam esse controversiam in locum jam dictum Bellarmini scribens. Neque multum discrepat a Bellarminiana definitio illa, quam tanquam planiorem, & pleniorem illi substituit; videlicet quod sit potentia volendi, nolendi, eligendi, repudiandi objectum ab intellectu monstratum, sine coactione, spontaneo ac deliberato motu, & aptitudine voluntatis ad volendum, aut nolendum opposita. Et similiter Amesius fatetur istam definitionem illum sensum habere posse, ut de ea non sit contendendi causa. in Bell. enerv. tom. 4. lib. 4. cap. 1.
pass_a_gloss: But however the Doctors of the Reformed School vary among themselves, in explaining what the nature of liberty is, & to what faculties it belongs, or does not belong; they nevertheless readily admit the definition of free Choice which is given by Bellarmine, On Grace & free Choice book 3. chap. 3. Namely that Free Choice is a free power of choosing from those things which conduce to some end one before another, or of rejecting, or accepting one & the same thing, at our discretion, attributed, or granted to intelligent nature, to the great glory of God. This may be seen in Rob. Baron in his general Metaphysics, sect. 12. Disp. on Liberty of Choice, where he not only approves this definition, but also explains it accurately by parts. The same definition also Pareus does not disapprove, since having made certain remarks upon it, he confesses that about free Choice absolutely considered, there is no controversy between us & Bellarmine writing on the place of Bellarmine already mentioned. Nor does that definition differ much from the Bellarminian, which he substitutes for it as plainer, & fuller; namely that it is the power of willing, not willing, choosing, rejecting an object shown by the intellect, without coaction, by spontaneous and deliberate motion, & with an aptitude of the will for willing, or not willing the opposite. And similarly Ames confesses that this definition can have that sense, that there is no cause of contending about it. in Bell. enerv. tom. 4. book 4. chap. 1.
pass_b_english: However the teachers of the Reformed school differ in explaining the nature of freedom and the faculties it does or does not belong to, they readily accept Bellarmine's definition of free choice in On Grace and Free Choice (book 3, chapter 3): "Free choice is the free power, given or granted to an intelligent nature for the great glory of God, of choosing among things that lead to some end one rather than another, or of rejecting or accepting one and the same thing, as we judge fit."

Robert Baron shows this in his General Metaphysics (section 12, disputation On Freedom of Choice), where he not only approves the definition but explains it carefully part by part. Pareus does not reject it either. Commenting on that passage of Bellarmine, he makes some remarks on the definition and then admits that, on free choice considered absolutely, there is no dispute between us and Bellarmine.

The definition Pareus puts in its place as plainer and fuller is not far from Bellarmine's: free choice is "the power of willing, not willing, choosing or rejecting an object the intellect sets before it, without compulsion, by a spontaneous and deliberate movement, with the will able to will or not will the opposite." Likewise Ames grants that the definition can bear a sense that leaves no reason to quarrel over it (Bellarmine Disarmed, volume 4, book 4, chapter 1).

choices.term: aptitudine voluntatis ad volendum, aut nolendum opposita
choices.english: with the will able to will or not will the opposite
choices.why: Pareus adds the will's standing capacity for the opposite as the mark of strict freedom; 'able to will or not will the opposite' keeps it.
